findings.text: The first sentence of the page says plainly what Athena is and what makes it different. A newcomer can say what Athena is after reading one paragraph.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: This is Athena's site, but the title and almost all of the page are about another project, firstmate, which a newcomer has never heard of. Someone who came to learn about Athena gets three lead paragraphs about it and then a long technical study of a different tool.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The page gives a reason for the study: it shows that Athena can explain code with sources. But the lead says Athena's main job is turning a request into a code change, and the page never shows that happening. The demonstration covers a side ability, not the main one.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: The next step is easy to find. It is linked from the top of the page, and the Next steps section gives a repository link, an install command and a sample command.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and heading "Next steps"

findings.text: The install step does not list prerequisites, such as the Rust toolchain or which AI model accounts or keys are needed. It also does not say what to expect after running `athena ask`. A newcomer may get stuck or not know whether it worked.
findings.source: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" / "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The middle of the page has states, a counter, eleven transition cards, exit codes and lock behaviour. That detail suits someone running firstmate, but it is far too dense for a newcomer deciding whether Athena is worth trying.
findings.source: Heading "Transitions" — "t2 queued → queued ... the spawn is deferred with exit 75"

findings.text: The Start here section is well built. It gives a one-sentence definition of firstmate, defines the key words up front, and walks through one task in order. A reader who wants to understand firstmate has a clear way in.
findings.source: Heading "Start here" — "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails"

findings.text: The page says openly that nothing was run and that a first reading missed several paths. This helps a newcomer trust the claims, though they may not see why an admitted miss is a selling point.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study" — "This study read the pinned tree only... every claim is marked read."

findings.text: The same definitions appear two or three times: the yolo, green, red and in scope entries show up under Words used first, in the main text and again in the Glossary. Some entries also define a term mostly by what is not known. Together this makes the page longer and harder to skim.
findings.source: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."
